newsitem.title: UK: Day of reckoning nears for Clyde Petroleum.
newsitem.headline: Day of reckoning nears for Clyde Petroleum.

text.p: The bid battle for Clyde Petroleum Plc was entering its final stages on Friday with industry watchers still undecided whether the 494 million pound ($801 million) hostile bid by Gulf Canada Resources' was enough to win over shareholders.

One of Clyde's major shareholders, PDFM, has already sold its 14.9 percent stake to Gulf at the 1.20 pounds per share offer, but other institutional investors are biding their time before the Tuesday deadline.
Analysts were unwilling to speculate about the outcome of what has been one of the fiercest takeover wars seen in the British oil exploration and production sector in recent years.
Schroders Plc, Clyde's largest shareholder with a 19.5 percent stake, was reported to be sticking with the takeover target, but a source at the fund manager declined to confirm this.
"We will decide by Tuesday," he said.

Gulf Canada, which earlier this month raised its bid from an original 105 pence per share, has had a hard time winning investor support, but suddenly made strong progress earlier this week as crude oil prices weakened.
PDFM and other investors sold in the open market, leaving Gulf Canada with 29.9 percent of Clyde, the maximum level a bidder is allowed to buy in the market under British rules.

The chances of a white knight stepping in at the last minute to top Gulf's offer are now seen as very slim -- as suggested by the Clyde share price, whichclosed at 117 pence on Friday, just below the level of the Gulf bid.
"We are not popping champagne corks here yet, but we are quietly confident that we have made a very good case out there," said Dick Auchinleck, vice president international of Gulf Canada.
Clyde Petroleum, meanwhile reiterated its argument that Gulf's offer was too low.
"Those who will support Clyde will see a very bright future," managing director Roy Franklin said.

Analysts were divided, some saying that it was better to accept Gulf Canada's cash rather than seeing Clyde's share price slip if the bid failed. The shares traded at 84-1/2 pence just before Gulf Canada first expressed its takeover interest.
Other analysts said the offer lacked a takeover premium.
"All of the alternative investments (in the oil exploration and production sector) are trading on similar valuations as Clyde," said Paul Spedding at Kleinwort Benson.
Ploughing back the bid proceeds in the attractive oil exploration sector would send shares soaring and this prospect may deter investors from parting with Clyde, he added.
"If Schroders take the cash they won't be able to put it back into the sector -- not at current prices," Spedding said.
"The key issue now is the reinvestment question," he added.
The E&P sector has been one of the best performing on the London stock exchange after being fuelled by takeover bid hopes following a flurry of acquisitions since late 1995.
With a flow of positive announcements on new oil finds, the sector has continued its bull run this year and many pundits see further gains ahead.
But with oil prices falling since the beginning of 1997, it will likely not be easy for investors to decide whether to hold on to or sell their Clyde shares.
"It is going to be close, but I believe we have a very good chance," said Clyde's Franklin. ($1=.6167 Pound)
